related_questions.question: What is the new HIV treatment 2025?

text_blocks.snippet: In 2025, significant advancements in HIV treatment and prevention include the FDA approval of lenacapavir (Yeztugo) for both treatment and prevention, with a twice-yearly injectable option. Additionally, new long-acting antiretroviral drugs like VH-184 and VH-499 are showing promising results in clinical trials, potentially offering new long-acting injectable treatment options. Research is also progressing towards a potential HIV cure, with studies exploring ways to force the virus out of hiding within cells and make it visible for potential eradication.
snippet_highlighted_words: lenacapavir (Yeztugo) for both treatment and prevention, with a twice-yearly injectable option

list.title: FDA Approval:
list.snippet: Lenacapavir, an injectable HIV-1 capsid inhibitor, received FDA approval for both HIV prevention (as PrEP) and treatment for those with drug-resistant HIV.

list.title: Prevention:
list.snippet: As PrEP, it offers a twice-yearly injectable option, providing 6 months of protection with a single dose.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: Lenacapavir is also approved for treatment, including for individuals with HIV resistant to other therapies.

list.title: Efficacy:
list.snippet: Clinical trials (PURPOSE 1 and PURPOSE 2) demonstrated high efficacy in preventing new HIV infections with lenacapavir, with virtually no infections among those on the drug, according to NPR.

list.title: WHO Recommendation:
list.snippet: The World Health Organization (WHO) also recommended lenacapavir for HIV prevention.

list.title: VH-184 and VH-499:
list.snippet: These drugs, in early clinical trials, demonstrated similar potency to existing antiretrovirals, with potential for long-acting injectable administration.

list.title: Need for New Drugs:
list.snippet: The development of new long-acting treatments is crucial for individuals who develop resistance or experience side effects with current therapies.

list.title: Forcing the Virus Out of Hiding:
list.snippet: Researchers are exploring ways to make the HIV virus visible within cells, potentially allowing for its eradication.

list.title: Understanding the Viral Reservoir:
list.snippet: Studies are focusing on understanding how the virus hides within cells and how to reactivate it for potential elimination.

list.title: mRNA Technology:
list.snippet: Researchers are using mRNA technology, similar to that used in some COVID-19 vaccines, to make the virus visible.

list.title: Hope for a Cure:
list.snippet: These advancements are raising hopes for a potential cure for HIV.

related_questions.question: What is the new breakthrough in HIV treatment?
related_questions.snippet: The FDA has approved a breakthrough preventative treatment for HIV that could change the course of the AIDS epidemic. But deep cuts to health initiatives could hinder the rollout. Lenacapavir not only offers nearly 100 percent protection from HIV, but people only need two injections per year.

related_questions.question: Will there be a cure for HIV in 2030?

text_blocks.snippet: While there's no definitive cure for HIV currently, research offers hope for a potential cure by 2030, but it's not guaranteed. The focus is on achieving "functional cures" through strategies like immunotherapy and gene therapy, rather than eradicating the virus entirely. However, meeting the broader goal of ending the HIV epidemic by 2030, which includes preventing new infections and ensuring access to treatment, faces significant challenges.
snippet_highlighted_words: research offers hope for a potential cure by 2030, but it's not guaranteed

list.title: Current Treatment:
list.snippet: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is the standard treatment for HIV, effectively managing the virus and allowing people to live long, healthy lives. However, ART needs to be taken daily for life.

list.title: Cure Research:
list.snippet: Research is actively exploring various approaches to cure HIV, including:
Immunotherapy: Boosting the immune system to fight off the virus.
Gene Therapy: Modifying the patient's genes to make them resistant to HIV.
mRNA Technology: Using mRNA to instruct cells to produce proteins that can combat the virus.
Complexity of the Virus: HIV is a complex virus that can hide in reservoirs within the body, making it difficult to eliminate.
Scalability: Many promising approaches, like stem cell transplants, are not easily scalable to the millions of people living with HIV worldwide.
Financial and logistical hurdles: Ensuring access to potential cures for all who need them will require significant resources and infrastructure.

list.title: Progress:
list.snippet: Partial successes have been reported in some individuals, offering hope for future breakthroughs. However, these cases are often complex and not readily transferable to a general cure.

list.title: Ending the Epidemic:
list.snippet: The broader goal of ending the HIV epidemic by 2030, as set by the UN, includes preventing new infections, ensuring access to testing and treatment, and reducing stigma. While progress has been made in reducing new infections, the world is currently off track to meet the 2030 target.

related_questions.question: How many years does an HIV patient live with treatment?

text_blocks.snippet: With effective HIV treatment (antiretroviral therapy or ART), people with HIV can now expect to live a near-normal lifespan. Life expectancy for people on treatment is now comparable to that of the general population, with some studies showing similar or even slightly longer lifespans.
snippet_highlighted_words: people with HIV can now expect to live a near-normal lifespan

list.title: Significant Improvements:
list.snippet: Due to advancements in HIV treatment, particularly the introduction of potent and well-tolerated ART, life expectancy for people with HIV has dramatically increased.

list.title: Near-Normal Lifespan:
list.snippet: Studies indicate that people with HIV who start and maintain effective treatment can expect to live as long as HIV-negative individuals.
Early Treatment: Starting ART promptly after diagnosis is crucial. Early initiation can lead to better health outcomes and a longer lifespan.
CD4 Count: The CD4 count (a measure of immune system health) at the start of treatment and during treatment also influences life expectancy.
Viral Load: Achieving and maintaining viral suppression (undetectable viral load) through ART is vital for long-term health.
Other Factors: Age at diagnosis, overall health, access to quality healthcare, and adherence to treatment also play a role.

list.title: Example:
list.snippet: One study found that a 20-year-old starting ART after 2008 could expect to live to about 78, similar to the average life expectancy in the US, according to a YouTube video about HIV life expectancy. Another study showed that a 35-year-old with HIV who achieved viral suppression and a CD4 count of at least 350 cells/µl within a year of starting ART could expect to live to about 80 years of age, according to a study published in AIDS.

list.title: Continued Monitoring and Care:
list.snippet: Regular check-ups, adherence to medication, and addressing any other health issues are essential for maintaining a long and healthy life with HIV.
